claims.text: The selected quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys can all be prepared as single-phase FCC microstructures after identical thermomechanical processing.
Mechanical-property differences among the quinary alloy and its subsets arise primarily from variations in local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortions alter the stacking-fault-energy landscape.
Variations in stacking-fault energy modulate the activation of dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
Increasing compositional complexity increases variation in local interatomic distances.
The quinary alloy has a broader distribution of local stacking-fault energies than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
A broader local stacking-fault-energy distribution promotes deformation-twin nucleation.
Pronounced twin formation enhances work hardening in the quinary alloy.
Activation of multiple slip systems contributes to enhanced work hardening in the quinary alloy.
Differences in constituent-atom lattice parameters hinder partial-dislocation motion through friction and thereby harden CoNiCrFeMn.
Higher compositional complexity produces greater dislocation friction than occurs in the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Removing constituents from the quinary alloy reduces local lattice distortion.
Removing constituents produces a more spatially uniform stacking-fault energy.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will have lower strength than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit less deformation twinning than the quinary baseline.
Quaternary and ternary subsets may have greater ductility than the quinary baseline.
Strength, ductility, work hardening, and twinning activity should correlate quantitatively with lattice-distortion metrics and stacking-fault-energy homogeneity.
The proposed mechanism is limited to alloys that remain single-phase FCC and do not undergo phase separation or intermetallic formation.
Lower-cost subsets would offer favorable cost-performance if their mechanical-property reductions remain acceptable for structural use.
